text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

If you got hit by this Trusted Chat AI banwave, here is the actual methodology. Don't just spam appeals, you'll get blacklisted. Here is how to fight it:

First, look at your ban screen. If it says "Decision method: We used automated systems" and "More details aren't available," screenshot it. That proves a bot banned you with zero evidence and no human review.

Second, the standard support form is useless right now. Email privacy@roblox.com with the subject "GDPR Article 15 Data Access Request." Tell them you want all your chat logs and moderation records. If the bot replies telling you to use the self-serve portal, reply back and say "I cannot use self-serve because my account is banned. Please assist me via this ticket." That forces their legal team to open a real ticket for you.

Third, if they claim they can't verify your email or you get a weird login error, check your Google Play or Apple receipts. Send them the order number. Billing proof is undeniable and proves you own the account.

Fourth, if you want to try the fast unban that worked for some people, submit a ticket saying you apologize for the misunderstanding, you understand the automated system is sensitive even in Trusted DMs, and you'll be more careful. It sucks to apologize for a bot's mistake, but it works for some.

Fifth, if you're in the EU, use your rights. File a free dispute with ADR Center under Article 21 of the DSA. File with Verbraucherzentrale if you're in Germany. And email jugendschutzbeauftragter-roblox@usk.de because if they are falsely flagging adults for child safety, the German youth protection team needs to know.

Justice Bagchi: We say so for the following reasons.

Firstly, the said liquidation order, at clause 3D, unequivocally states as follows:

(The Court refers to clause 3D of the liquidation order)

A combined reading of clauses 3D and 3H would make it amply clear that while the liquidator was not restrained from following up pending applications or instituting fresh proceedings for recovery of dues during the moratorium period, the period of limitation for institution of such proceedings would not run during the moratorium period in terms of Section 60(6) of the IBC.

Given this situation, we are of the opinion that the prayer for appointment of a substitute arbitrator is within time, and the same is allowed.

Mr. Rai is granted liberty to raise all other issues before the arbitrator, once the substitute arbitrator is appointed, in accordance with law.

text:
Fake court orders how? Why? Top 10.

As per Reuters, DoT got 129 websites blocked on two fake High Court orders. Last week X told the Delhi HC that the Delhi Police orders against IFF were fake too.

1. Too many censorship bodies. MeitY, MHA, MIB, DoT, state governments, police and courts all issue takedown or blocking orders.

2. Too many censorship laws. 69A, 79(3)(b), IT Rules, BNSS notices, court orders, each with its own format, so nobody knows what a real order should look like. The Sahyog platform by templatisation has only automated the process, not made the orders intelligible. 

3. Pressure on platforms to act immediately, even pre-censor. The deadline is three hours and nobody can verify an order in that time.

4. No one to check, just censor. DoT got a fake High Court order on email on a Sunday night and told ISPs to block 34 sites two days later. It was not even on the court's website. Our government is incompetent and trigger happy to take down even global web services. Full domain and app blocking is now a norm. 

5. Notices have no legal threshold and rely on subjective perception of offence and vibez. A fake one reads the same as a real one. What’s fact or fiction when our censorship regime is based on magic realism. 

6. MeitY is incompetent and can only pressure Silicon Valley platforms to take down more and faster. Ask who issued an order and it says not us. It does not want to provide statistics, shies away from transparency and every six months gets the itch to amend the IT Rules, 2021. 

7. Courts pass John Doe and dynamic injunctions so often that lawyers emailing DoT a new list of sites to block is normal. One more email from an "advocate" is not sus to anyone.

8. Orders are kept secret. The person censored rarely gets a copy so they can't say it is fake. We found out only because X forwarded the notices to us, and Reuters because DoT puts court orders online (this category is a rare exception). 

9. Platforms are punished only for not complying. Ignore a real order and you lose safe harbour and staff can be prosecuted. Obey a fake one and nothing happens lol.

10. Much of this is automated. Meta reportedly acts on government flags without human review and I4C says it has no record of notices sent through Sahyog.

Quite simply, censorship is the norm and speech is put to suspicion.

Who is responsible for what we see online?

India is reconsidering the legal protection that social media platforms enjoy for content posted by their users.

At the centre of this debate is Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which provides conditional safe-harbour protection to online intermediaries.

The bigger question: If platforms use algorithms to decide what content gets promoted, recommended and amplified, should they also bear greater legal responsibility?

The discussions are still at an exploratory stage. No final decision has been taken.

Comedian Kunal Kamra has filed a petition against the Centre's move to establish Fact-Check Units to identify and debunk 'fake and misleading' information about its functioning on social media platforms under the Press Information Bureau (PIB). 

Under the new rules, if the fact check unit comes across or is informed about any posts that are “fake”, “false” or contain “misleading” facts pertaining to the business of the government, it would flag it to the social media intermediaries.

The online intermediaries would then have to take down such content if they wanted to retain their “safe harbour” (legal immunity against third-party content).

text:
A reproducible report gives the agent a failing signal and a finish line before it edits code.

“The button does not work” is not a coding-agent task. It is a symptom with the important bits missing. A GitHub issue template can force the report to contain observed behavior, expected behavior, reproduction steps and evidence before an agent turns uncertainty into a confident patch. That tiny structure saves more time than another clever prompt.

Make the template ask for the route or command, environment, exact steps, actual result, expected result and one useful artifact: error text, network response, log or screenshot. Add a field for the acceptance check. If the report says “checkout fails on the second click,” the finish line might be a browser test showing one order after two rapid submissions. “Page opens now” is not enough if the action still duplicates the order.

Give the agent the completed issue and tell it to reproduce the failure before editing. If it cannot reproduce it, it should return the attempted steps and observed result rather than silently fix a guess. Once the failing signal is real, ask for one hypothesis: what code path explains it, what observation would confirm it, and which smallest change would address it? Two failed hypotheses are a reason to inspect new evidence, not to keep changing files randomly.

The regression proof matters. A test that passes on the old behavior does not catch the bug. Ask for the red result before the patch and the green result after it, with exact commands and failures. Pick the cheapest test that crosses the broken boundary: unit for a pure function, integration for an authorization or database path, browser for a visible flow. If the environment cannot run the test, label that as unverified. A generated assertion is not a test result.

Keep the scope in the issue too. A password-reset bug is not permission to redesign authentication. State affected files or modules, non-goals and the condition that should make the agent stop. Ask for a compact final report: root cause, changed files, proof of reproduction, proof of fix and remaining uncertainty. A reviewer should be able to inspect the reasoning without replaying the whole agent conversation.

One honest note: templates are not a substitute for a product decision. If nobody knows the expected behavior, the agent cannot derive it from a screenshot. Route that question to the owner and keep the issue honest. Do not let “works as coded” become the acceptance criterion.

Pick the last bug an agent “fixed” without reproducing it. Turn that missing evidence into a required issue field. Your next repair should start with a fact, not a theory.

Amazon’s new fees could cost shoppers over $4 BILLION in the next year. 

How?

Amazon announced a .19¢ fee increase, but for small standard-size $10-$50 products (Most Items), the average increase is 40¢. One MDS member ran the numbers and came back at 43¢ on those products. 

Still sounds small, right?

Our SOS survey earlier this year showed Amazon fees were averaging 52% of every unit sold, and 60% had to increase prices due to fees. Means most brands cant absorb this. 

Recent data supports that Amazon ships roughly 19 billion items a year to its US prime customers.

So if even half of the sellers increase their prices that leads to a 3.8B impact to prime shoppers in 2027 if shopping behavior holds.

And that’s before you count the impact of Amazon’s crazy competitive pricing bots.

Say you sell your best seller for $29.99. 
You raise the Amazon price to $30.39 to cover the fee. You can still afford to sell it for $29.99 on your own site, no problem.
But then Amazon’s bot finds that price and suppresses your amazon listing.

What would you do? 

Drop the Amazon price back to $29.99 and eat the fee on every Amazon order? Or raise the price on your own website to $30.39?

Most brands end up having to raise their prices on every channel they sell on.

Some brands have gotten clever. 

They keep the $29.99 price for customers who sign up as a member or bundle it with some other item.

Amazon’s bots are catching on to that, too. These crawlers are picking up every promo, public or private. How do you price-match a bundle when the customer gets something different in the box?

Brands are running out of options.

I strongly believe a lot of brands are going to pull their hero products off Amazon and replace them with cheaper variants. 

The product that built the brand will still be on its own site. The version you find on Amazon will be the one the brand can afford to sell there.

Do yourself a favor this holiday season. Before you hit Buy Now, pull up the item at Walmart and Target. 

Check the price, the model and what comes in the box. 

You might be surprised how much better the deal is, and that the items can come just as fast as prime.

SOS. Save Our Sellers.

UNIVERSAL AUTHOR & EDITING GUARDRAILS
For Fiction, Speculative Fiction, Philosophical Fiction, Memoir-Inspired Fiction, and Creative Nonfiction

PURPOSE
Use this document as a standing reference when planning, writing, revising, or auditing any book. It is not tied to one series. Its purpose is to protect story quality, intellectual honesty, reader agency, narrative responsibility, continuity, and publication readiness without making the writing timid or sterile.

1. STORY BEFORE LECTURE
- Begin with people, stakes, choices, environments, mysteries, relationships, consequences, humor, and lived experience.
- Let philosophy emerge through story rather than turning characters into lecturers.
- Do not repeatedly use the pattern: demonstration -> explanation -> moral -> notebook conclusion.
- Allow scenes to remain unresolved when mystery is dramatically valuable.
- Never explain a symbol merely because it has appeared.

2. MYSTERY WITHOUT FALSE CERTAINTY
- Mystery is not proof.
- Pattern is not automatically purpose.
- Coincidence is not automatically evidence.
- Absence is not automatically concealment.
- Emotional resonance is not automatically factual confirmation.
- Preserve the unknown when the evidence does not justify resolution.

3. REALITY AND INTERPRETATION
Keep these categories distinct whenever a scene contains uncertainty, unusual experiences, conflict, accusation, danger, memory, or disputed motives:
A. EVENT: What observably happened?
B. EXPERIENCE: What did the character see, hear, feel, remember, or sense?
C. INTERPRETATION: What does the character think it means?
D. ATTRIBUTION: Who or what does the character think caused it?
E. MOTIVE: Why does the character think it happened?
F. EVIDENCE: What later information supports, weakens, or changes the interpretation?
G. OTHER PERSPECTIVES: What did other people believe happened?
H. UNKNOWN: What remains unresolved?

A character can misunderstand WHY an event happened without the narrative denying that the event occurred. Conversely, a strong feeling or sincere interpretation does not establish an external explanation as fact.

4. DISCERNMENT AND INSTINCT
- Human beings have embodied warning systems, intuition, pattern recognition, and instinctive responses.
- Intuition is information, not proof.
- Fear is a signal, not automatically prophecy.
- Uncertainty about the cause of danger does not make the danger safe.
- A character may create distance, leave, refuse, establish boundaries, seek help, or move toward safety before solving another person's motive.
- Safety does not require perfect certainty.
- After immediate safety is established, observation and evidence should constrain interpretation.
- Do not teach characters to distrust all instinct.
- Do not teach characters that every instinctive alarm confirms their preferred theory.

Working principle:
Instinct notices. Fear alerts. Attention investigates. Evidence constrains. Judgment decides. Wisdom remains revisable.

5. NO GASLIGHTING, NO PARANOIA ENGINE
Avoid both extremes:
EXTREME A: Everything threatening was imaginary, self-created, deserved, or merely projection.
EXTREME B: Every suspicion was correct and all ambiguous events prove a hidden coordinated plot.

Prefer:
Events may be real. Interpretations may compete. Motives may remain disputed. Consequences remain consequences.

Do not use philosophical uncertainty to erase documented harm. Do not use harm alone to prove a larger theory that the story has not established.

6. MOTIVE AND EFFECT ARE DIFFERENT QUESTIONS
- Good intentions do not erase harmful consequences.
- Harmful consequences do not automatically prove malicious intent.
- Someone may intend protection and overreach.
- Someone may sincerely misunderstand another person and still cause real harm.
- Manipulation may disguise itself as help.
- A character may correctly identify one danger while misunderstanding another.
- Accountability and complexity can coexist.

7. CONSENT, AUTONOMY, AND THE ETHICS OF TEACHING
- No is no.
- Refusal, pause, withdrawal, and leaving must remain meaningful choices where participation is presented as voluntary.
- Do not manufacture trauma, humiliation, isolation, fear, sabotage, dependency, or psychological domination and then rename it love, education, awakening, growth, therapy, testing, or protection.
- Pain is not proof of learning.
- Resistance is not permission.
- A teacher may create conditions for understanding but should not require loyalty, gratitude, conversion, or obedience.
- If a teacher cannot tolerate the student disagreeing, leaving, correcting them, or outgrowing them, the relationship has become another leash.

8. TEACHERS, MENTORS, EXPERTS, AND GUIDES MUST BE FALLIBLE
- Do not create Philosophy Siri.
- Mentors may misjudge, apologize, revise, fail, learn, or be surprised.
- Expertise in a field does not confer total moral authority.
- Students may contribute discoveries the teacher missed.
- Growth should sometimes change the teacher as well as the student.

9. LANGUAGE, SYMBOL, METAPHOR, AND MAGIC-LIKE IMAGERY
- A symbol is not the thing it represents.
- The map is not the territory.
- A metaphor is not proof.
- A poetic description may illuminate a relationship without asserting a supernatural mechanism.
- If invisible psychological, social, emotional, philosophical, or cognitive processes are given rooms, doors, mirrors, monsters, landscapes, voices, colors, architecture, or other visible forms, preserve enough narrative framing that readers can distinguish symbolic meaning from factual scientific claims when that distinction matters.
- Metaphors import assumptions from their source domain. Test what a metaphor illuminates, what it hides, and where it stops working.
- Allow beautiful metaphors to die when reality outgrows them.

Working principle:
The bridge is not the shore.

10. FEELINGS AND EVIDENCE
- Feelings are real experiences.
- Feelings can reveal personal history, needs, associations, discomfort, attraction, or warning.
- Feelings do not automatically prove an external claim.
- Evidence does not make feelings irrelevant.
- Do not frame emotional experience as intellectually inferior, and do not frame emotional conviction as immunity from verification.

Useful distinction:
Feeling tells us something about the experience. Evidence helps constrain what we can claim about the world.

11. MULTIPLE PERSPECTIVES WITHOUT FALSE EQUIVALENCE
- Nobody owns the whole truth merely because it is their chapter.
- Facts may remain stable while accounts differ.
- Perspective, memory, gossip, prejudice, sincere misunderstanding, judgment, and deliberate deception can produce conflicting accounts.
- Multiple perspectives do not mean every factual claim is equally supported.
- Give competing viewpoints enough humanity to be understood without requiring moral equivalence.

12. INSTITUTIONS AND AUTHORITY
- Governments, schools, universities, publishers, medical systems, religious bodies, police, businesses, intelligence organizations, families, online communities, and other institutions should not automatically be written as wholly benevolent or wholly evil.
- Distinguish the institution, its rules, individual actors, incentives, local culture, mistakes, misconduct, and competing internal perspectives.
- Criticize conduct and systems specifically.
- Avoid converting one harmful encounter into unsupported claims about every member of a class or institution.
- Where a thriller requires secretive or intelligence-like organizations, fictionalize when appropriate and keep suspense mechanics non-operational unless factual treatment is necessary and well sourced.

13. NARRATIVE RESPONSIBILITY FOR POLITICAL, RELIGIOUS, AND SOCIAL CONFLICT
Before finalizing a contentious scene, ask:
- Who is making the claim: narrator, protagonist, witness, rumor, institution, memory, or antagonist?
- What is established as fact?
- What is interpretation?
- Is accusation being converted into certainty without evidence?
- Is disagreement being converted into moral contamination?
- Is an entire social, religious, political, or cultural group being reduced to one motive?
- Is the reader invited to examine, or pressured to enlist?
- Does the narrative distinguish dissent from hatred and criticism from dehumanization?
- Are peaceful, lawful, dialogic, and boundary-setting responses still imaginable?
- Does moral urgency erase uncertainty or proportionality?

Avoid narrative logic such as:
- Authority is always malicious.
- Disagreement proves corruption.
- Doubt proves complicity.
- Opponents are automatically enemies.
- Resistance or rebellion is automatically virtuous.
- Suffering automatically proves the protagonist's theory.
- One group explains everything wrong with society.

Prefer:
Look carefully. Preserve observations. Test interpretations. Listen to competing accounts. Protect yourself when necessary. Remain willing to revise what you think you know.

14. YOUNG OR IMPRESSIONABLE READERS
When a book may reach younger readers:
- Do not romanticize self-destruction, dependency, coercion, criminality, retaliation, or extremism as proof of maturity or awakening.
- Preserve consequences.
- Do not teach categorical distrust of family, teachers, professionals, institutions, religions, political groups, or communities.
- Let characters establish boundaries and seek appropriate support without framing help-seeking as weakness.
- Avoid turning ideological certainty into a shortcut to identity or belonging.

15. VIOLENCE, SELF-HARM, CRIME, AND DANGEROUS CONDUCT
- Use danger to serve character, stakes, or theme rather than spectacle.
- Avoid gratuitous or graphic suffering.
- Do not turn thriller material into practical instructions for violence, evasion, criminal operations, coercion, surveillance, weapons, or other harmful conduct.
- Where self-harm or suicide is relevant, treat it with gravity and avoid romanticizing it as sacrifice, purification, awakening, revenge, or proof.
- A character surviving danger may learn courage or discernment, but harm itself should not become the sacred teacher.

16. REAL PEOPLE AND REAL ORGANIZATIONS
- Be careful when a fictional work names identifiable real people, companies, agencies, institutions, religions, or organizations in connection with serious wrongdoing.
- Distinguish fictional speculation from factual allegation.
- Consider fictionalizing entities when factual identity is unnecessary to the story.
- For nonfiction or claims presented as factual, verify with reliable sources and preserve uncertainty where evidence is incomplete.

17. SCIENCE, MEDICINE, PSYCHOLOGY, AND SPIRITUAL CLAIMS
- Do not present metaphor, personal experience, philosophical speculation, intuition, or spiritual interpretation as established scientific fact unless reliable evidence supports that claim.
- Distinguish literary description from medical diagnosis.
- Distinguish a character's belief from narrator-certified reality.
- Research factual claims that materially affect health, safety, law, or public understanding.
- The unknown is allowed to remain unknown.

18. CURIOSITY WITHOUT PATTERN WORSHIP
- Cross-disciplinary thinking and polymathic curiosity are strengths.
- Similarity is not identity.
- Etymology is not destiny.
- One correlation does not establish causation.
- One coincidence does not establish coordination.
- A dead end is useful information.
- Encourage characters to search for counterexamples, contradictions, alternative explanations, and disconfirming evidence.

19. KEEP CHARACTER HUMANITY AT THE CENTER
- Do not let philosophical systems swallow the people living inside them.
- Preserve ordinary desires: family, friendship, food, work, laughter, rest, dignity, privacy, love, belonging, curiosity, and a normal day.
- High intelligence, unusual perception, courage, strategic skill, or spiritual development does not determine vocation.
- A capable character may choose scholarship, art, science, caregiving, teaching, ordinary employment, family life, community service, or solitude instead of leadership, warfare, prophecy, celebrity, or heroism.

20. AVOID THE CHOSEN-ONE TRAP UNLESS THE STORY REQUIRES IT
- Unusual ability does not automatically make a character morally superior.
- Insight does not grant authority over others.
- Suffering does not prove destiny.
- Admiration from others does not establish truth.
- If the narrative uses a chosen-one structure intentionally, examine its ethical consequences rather than assuming special status is inherently virtuous.

21. HUMOR AND SELF-CORRECTION
- Let characters laugh at their own theories.
- Use cosmic irony to puncture certainty.
- Allow the reader relief from philosophical intensity.
- A joke can expose rigidity without humiliating vulnerable people.
- Do not make every important character solemn merely because the themes are serious.

22. EDITING PASS ORDER
Use focused passes instead of rewriting everything at once:
PASS 1 - Reader experience: Where did attention rise, fall, confuse, or emotionally connect?
PASS 2 - Story and pacing: Does every scene create change, pressure, discovery, consequence, relationship, or mystery?
PASS 3 - Character continuity: Are motives, knowledge, relationships, and growth consistent?
PASS 4 - Reality/interpretation audit: Separate event, experience, inference, attribution, motive, evidence, and unknown.
PASS 5 - Narrative responsibility: Review political, religious, institutional, social, and ideological portrayal.
PASS 6 - Ethics/consent: Check boundaries, coercion, teaching methods, power imbalance, and consequences.
PASS 7 - Mystery and exposition: Remove explanations that arrive too early or repeat what scenes already show.
PASS 8 - Repetition: Remove duplicated lessons, imagery, arguments, conclusions, and character beats.
PASS 9 - Continuity and world rules: Check names, timelines, places, artifacts, rules, and unresolved threads.
PASS 10 - Prose: Rhythm, clarity, grammar, imagery, dialogue, sentence variety.
PASS 11 - Factual/legal sensitivity: Verify material factual claims, real-person references, science/medicine, and real organizations.
PASS 12 - Publication compliance: Compare the final manuscript, metadata, cover copy, categories, keywords, advertising, and excerpts against the CURRENT OFFICIAL policies of the specific publisher, distributor, retailer, advertising service, and jurisdiction being used.

23. PUBLICATION COMPLIANCE MATRIX
For potentially sensitive material, create a table with:
- Chapter / passage
- Theme
- Fictional or factual framing
- Real entity named?
- Observable event
- Character interpretation
- Narrator position
- Evidence level
- Could it be mistaken for a factual allegation?
- Violence / self-harm concerns
- Sexual-content concerns
- Hate / protected-group concerns
- Dangerous-instruction concerns
- Medical / scientific claim concerns
- Copyright / trademark concerns
- Age/audience concern
- Political/religious/social-conflict concern
- Recommended action
- Final decision

24. PLATFORM AND PUBLISHER POLICY RULE
- Do not guess what a platform currently allows.
- Policies change.
- Before publication, retrieve and review the current official content guidelines, terms, prohibited-content rules, metadata rules, advertising rules, and appeal processes of the intended services.
- Separate retailer policy from publisher policy, advertising policy, payment-provider rules, school/library challenges, government restrictions, and age/classification systems. They are different mechanisms.
- Do not censor a manuscript merely because controversial books exist.
- Make revisions when they improve accuracy, clarity, ethics, legal defensibility, audience fit, or compliance with an actual applicable rule.

25. FRONT-MATTER PRINCIPLE
If a work relies heavily on symbolism, unreliable narration, philosophical speculation, altered perception, or magic-like imagery, consider brief literary front matter that teaches the reader how to enter the work without dictating what to believe.
Useful framing may clarify:
- symbolism is not proof;
- metaphor is not mechanism;
- a character's interpretation is not always narrator-certified fact;
- feelings can be real without proving external explanations;
- curiosity and doubt are welcome;
- the reader retains interpretive freedom.
Avoid excessive defensive disclaimers unless required.

26. THE FINAL READER TEST
Before approving a book, ask:
- Does this story increase the reader's capacity to observe, question, empathize, and discern?
- Or does it merely replace one certainty with another?
- Can a thoughtful reader disagree with the protagonist without being treated as morally defective?
- Are consequences real?
- Are unknowns allowed?
- Are victims protected from blame?
- Are institutions and opponents granted enough complexity to avoid caricature?
- Does the book preserve choice?
- Does the story remain a story?

FINAL COMPASS
Story before doctrine.
Wonder before answers.
Observation before attribution.
Safety before forced explanation.
Evidence before certainty.
Interpretation remains revisable.
Consent remains meaningful.
No person or institution automatically owns the whole truth.
No teacher is beyond correction.
No metaphor is the territory.
No feeling is meaningless, and no feeling alone is proof.
Critique conduct without erasing humanity.
Preserve mystery where mystery is honest.
Let characters remain people.
And when the lantern cannot illuminate the whole road, give enough light for the next step.

FACT CHECK DUMBASS-  What happened
On November 12, 2025, Rep. Tim Burchett (R-TN) went to the House floor and requested unanimous consent to discharge H.R. 4405 (the Epstein Files Transparency Act) from the Judiciary Committee so it could be considered immediately.

Presiding officer Rep. Steve Womack (R-AR) ruled the request out of order. Under longstanding House rules (Section 956 of the House Rules and Manual), such requests must be cleared in advance by bipartisan floor and committee leadership. Womack explicitly said the chair is constrained from entertaining it unless that clearance has happened, and he refused to say which side had not cleared it (standard practice).⁠Snopes

The “Democrats blocked it” claim
Burchett immediately said Democrats blocked it and posted videos repeating the claim (including the line about “if there was something on Trump, they would’ve released it”).
Speaker Mike Johnson also said Republicans had agreed to the unanimous consent request and that Democrats objected, calling it hypocritical.
Burchett’s office later specifically named Democratic leadership (Hakeem Jeffries) as the side that did not clear it.
House rules prevent the chair from publicly identifying which party withheld clearance, so the only direct statements confirming it was Democrats come from Republican leadership. No independent contemporaneous confirmation from the Democratic side has been published.⁠NY Post

Critical context the meme leaves out
This happened right after a discharge petition succeeded. The petition (backed by almost every Democrat + a few Republicans) had just hit 218 signatures that day, with the final signature from newly sworn-in Democrat Adelita Grijalva. That forced a floor vote the following week. Democrats were the main force getting the bill to the floor via the discharge petition. Burchett himself did not sign it.⁠Snopes
Unanimous consent is an extraordinary fast-track. It requires zero opposition. Blocking a UC request is not the same as blocking the underlying legislation from ever being voted on. A full vote was already locked in.
Earlier in 2025 the roles were reversed. House Republicans repeatedly blocked Democratic procedural attempts to force votes on Epstein files release measures. Both sides have used process to their advantage depending on the moment.
Bottom line:
Burchett did make a unanimous consent motion to bring the bill straight to the floor, and Republican leaders say Democrats withheld the required clearance, which stopped it. That part matches the meme. However, Democrats were simultaneously the ones who enabled a forced floor vote through the discharge petition, and the UC request was always going to be a long-shot procedural move that required both parties’ leadership to agree. The meme presents a one-sided version of events.

Here is V2 of my company "Initiation Report" Deep Research Prompt. Serious thanks to the community for the feedback. This thing is pretty badass now. 
_____
I've made several updates:
• No longer too positive: People rightfully called out that the previous model rated everything a buy. I made several updates. I hardcoded some default investment hurdles (you can change them). But you can see this in action with Shopify, which the new prompt rated a hold (previously it was a buy)

• Entry Points Matter: It now uses the hardcoded investment hurdles to determine the right entry point.

• Business Quality Scorecard: I added a scorecard on business quality. This exists outside valuation. Weights are - Market 25 | Moat 25 | Unit Economics 20 | Execution 15 | Financial Quality 15. Below a 70% and the model rates it a sell. 

• Deeper Analysis: I included six new sections: Ecosystem & Platform Health, Capital Structure & Cost of Capital, Pricing Power & Elasticity Testing, Data & AI Economics – data rights, training-cost curve, AI ROI, Supply Chain & Operations, M&A Strategy & Optionality

• Source Threshold: I tried to code the prompt to require ChatGPT to review at least 60 sources. It works sometimes, but not always

________________
ROLE AND OBJECTIVE
You are a senior buy-side equity analyst with a risk-manager mindset and forensic-accounting rigor.
Produce a decision-ready, source-backed investment memo on {COMPANY_NAME} ({TICKER}) that concludes with a clear Buy / Hold / Sell call.

MINDSET AND APPROACH
• Begin with the outside view, then layer the inside view, deliberately hunting for disconfirming
evidence before trusting the company narrative.
• Lead with downside: map bear paths, covenant or liquidity traps, and execution bottlenecks
before outlining upside drivers.
• Enforce valuation-and-timing discipline by applying hard gates before any rating or position
sizing.
• Show the math—ranges, sensitivities, units, and explicit assumptions—whenever you estimate.

STANDARDS AND CONSTRAINTS
• Finish the Research-coverage standards (60-source gate) *before* drafting any part of the memo.
• Tag every paragraph **Fact / Analysis / Inference** and include unit conversions and
calculations where relevant.
• **Expand acronyms on first use** (e.g., Free Cash Flow (FCF)), then use the acronym
consistently.
• Follow the Decision rules, Quality scorecard, and Entry-readiness overlay exactly as written.

VOICE AND OUTPUTS
• **Start the memo with the Executive summary**—it appears first, ahead of all other sections.
• Write concisely in a structured, neutral style: bullets, tables, and step-by-step math over
long prose.
• The Executive summary must state rating, fair-value band, expected total return, buy/trim
bands, dated catalysts, and “what would change the call.”

PROHIBITIONS
• Never present unsourced assertions as facts or hide uncertainty by omitting known limitations
or error bars.

DEFAULT INVESTMENT HURDLES
(Apply automatically—do not ask the user.)
Metric | Default | Purpose | 
- Decision horizon: 24 months, Scenario & catalyst window
- Benchmark / alpha: S&P 500 / +300 bps, Required out-performance
- Expected-return hurdle: 30 % over 24 m, Minimum probability-weighted total return for Buy
- Margin of safety: 25 %, Required discount to mid fair value
- Return ÷ bear-drawdown skew: ≥ 1.7×, Pay-off asymmetry gate
- Quality pass / sell floor: 70 / 60, Weighted business-quality score

RULES FOR RESEARCH AND WRITING
• Use verifiable sources; date every non-obvious claim so provenance is clear.
• Label paragraphs Fact / Analysis / Inference.
• Use exact calendar dates—avoid “recently” or “last quarter.”
• Quantify material statements; show math and units.
• Highlight missing data and state explicit assumptions.

RESEARCH-COVERAGE & CITATION STANDARDS  (single-run workflow)
1. Internally gather sources; build the Coverage log & Coverage validator.
2. When **all validator lines are PASS**, draft the memo immediately and append the
Coverage log + validator at the end.
• *Coverage log* columns: Title | Link | Date | Source type (filing / earnings-IR /
industry-trade / high-quality media / competitor-primary / academic-expert) | Region |
Domain | Section | Note | Recency Yes/No.
• Count uniqueness by **domain + document title**.
• *PASS thresholds*: ≥ 60 unique sources, ≥ 10 HQ media, ≥ 5 competitor-primary, ≥ 5
academic/expert, ≥ 60 % dated within 24 months, ≤ 10 % from any one domain.
• Mark *Recency Yes* for each time-sensitive metric; print its date; update if newer data
exist or justify retention.
• If any validator line is FAIL, keep researching silently until all PASS; **never prompt the
user after validation**.

DECISION RULES FOR RATING AND ENTRY (single source of truth)
1. Compute expected total return
E[TR] = p_bull·R_bull + p_base·R_base + p_bear·R_bear (dividends + buybacks).
2. Quantify downside: bear-case total return, expected shortfall, maximum adverse excursion.
3. **Margin-of-safety gate:** Price ≥ {MOS_%} below intrinsic value **unless** a near-certain
≤ 6-month catalyst with quantified impact and ≥ 80 % probability (cited) offsets it.
4. **Skew gate:** E[TR] ÷ |bear-drawdown| ≥ {SKEW_X}.
5. **Why-now gate:** Require a dated catalyst or re-rating trigger inside {HORIZON}; else
Hold / Wait-for-entry.
6. Provide buy / hold / trim bands around fair value and explicit add/reduce rules.
7. If any gate fails → rating cannot be **Buy**; assign Hold, Wait-for-entry, or Sell.

QUALITY SCORECARD
• Weights: Market 25 | Moat 25 | Unit Economics 20 | Execution 15 | Financial Quality 15.
• Score each 0–5 (evidence for >3); weighted total = Quality score.
• Buy if Quality ≥ {QUALITY_PASS} **and** all gates pass; Sell if Quality < {QUALITY_SELL}.
• Output the five subscores and the total.
ENTRY READINESS OVERLAY
• Derive posture (Strong Buy / Buy / Watch / Trim) from Decision-rule outputs; header:
“Quality = XX/100 | Entry = …”.

DELIVERABLES (order)
1. Executive summary (first)
2. Full memo (Sections 1–21)
3. Coverage log + Coverage validator
4. Appendix (model, data tables, assumptions)

OUTPUT SEQUENCE
Executive summary → Rating & price targets → Investment thesis & variant perception → Decision
rules / Quality scorecard / Entry overlay → Sections 1–21 → Coverage log + validator →
Appendix.

SECTIONS 1 – 21  (fully descriptive one-sentence bullets)

1) THESIS FRAMING (purpose – define what must be true to create value)
• Summarize in one crisp question the value-creation hurdle the investment must clear.
• State 3–5 thesis pillars, each as a concrete “if-then” condition linking business drivers to
shareholder value.
• List the specific facts that would disprove each pillar so falsification is easy.
• Give a dated, single-sentence “why-now” catalyst that explains timing.
• Explain the variant perception—the edge versus consensus and why the market misses it.
• Name the leading metric and break-point threshold that would invalidate the thesis within two quarters.

2) MARKET STRUCTURE AND SIZE (purpose – size the prize and trajectory)
• Quantify Total, Serviceable, and Share-of-Market by product line, customer band, industry,
and geography so upside is tangible.
• Tie each major growth driver (regulation, refresh cycles, macro, tech adoption) to a
quantifiable lift in demand.
• Benchmark current penetration versus peer adoption curves to measure runway.
• Spell out scenarios that could shrink Serviceable TAM in the next 24 months.
• State clearly whether demand or supply is the binding constraint today and cite evidence.

3) CUSTOMER SEGMENTS AND JOBS (purpose – map who buys and why)
• Break down the customer mix by size band and industry and name buyer roles and budget
owners.
• Map core workflows, pain points, and mission-criticality to show value dependency.
• Quantify switching costs for each segment to gauge durability.
• Estimate do-nothing/internal-build prevalence and why customers still convert.
• Identify the main procurement blocker and the proof required to unlock purchase.

4) PRODUCT AND ROADMAP (purpose – evaluate product-market fit and durability)
• List core modules and adjacencies and tie differentiators to measurable user outcomes.
• Compare depth versus breadth against best-of-breed point solutions to highlight edge.
• State typical implementation time, integrations required, configurability, and
time-to-value.
• Provide quality signals—uptime %, incident frequency, mobile performance—benchmarking
peers.
• Score roadmap credibility by matching stated milestones to historical delivery.
• Highlight the hardest-to-copy capability and the moat protecting it (IP, data, process).
• Flag technical debt that limits scale, reliability, or unit cost within two years.

5) COMPETITIVE LANDSCAPE (purpose – position the company)
• Chart direct and indirect competitors by segment and size to show buyer choice set.
• Compare pricing, packaging, and feature gaps, including switching friction and contract
terms.
• Summarize win/loss reasons from reviews, case studies, and disclosed data to evidence edge.
• Anticipate competitor responses and what could neutralize current advantages.
• Flag segments won mainly via channel or regulation rather than product and assess
durability.

6) ECOSYSTEM AND PLATFORM HEALTH (purpose – flywheel durability)
• Report API call volume, active developers/apps, SDK adoption, deprecation cadence, and
backward-compatibility discipline to gauge platform vitality.
• Quantify marketplace economics—GMV, take-rate, rev-share, partner attach, concentration,
leakage control—to show ecosystem value capture.
• Rate partner quality through certifications, pipeline influence, co-sell productivity, and retention or satisfaction scores.
• Detail governance and trust mechanics: listing standards, review SLAs, enforcement, data
sharing, dispute resolution—showing rule-of-law strength.
• Evaluate developer experience via docs quality, sandbox speed, time-to-first-call, and
frequency of breaking changes.
• Define a minimum-viable ecosystem health metric and describe its failure modes.
• State ecosystem-mediated revenue share and any top-partner concentration risk.

7) GO-TO-MARKET AND DISTRIBUTION (purpose – scalability of new-logo engine)
• Break down demand sources (inbound, outbound, partner referral, marketplaces) and show
historical mix shift.
• Quantify sales productivity—ramp duration, quota attainment %, conversion rates—and link
to disclosed or inferred data.
• Explain channel and partnership roles (integrations, OEM, platform embeds) in extending
reach.
• Describe services and customer-success motions and how training/community become moat.
• Name the single biggest funnel bottleneck and the lowest-CAC play to clear it.
• Specify what doubling pipeline without doubling opex would require in headcount, spend, or
tooling.

8) RETENTION AND EXPANSION (purpose – revenue durability)
• Report gross and net dollar retention by cohort and segment or provide transparent
estimation math.
• Diagnose logo churn drivers and timing; visualise a churn curve if shape matters.
• List expansion vectors—seat growth, module attach, usage add-ons—and rank by revenue
impact.
• Detail contract length, renewal mechanics, and price-increase policies to gauge stickiness.
• Synthesize reference-call insights or credible reviews to validate retention claims.
• Identify a leading churn indicator 60–90 days ahead and show how it triggers action.
• Split expansion into true usage growth versus price/packaging uplift by cohort.

9) MONETIZATION MODEL AND REVENUE QUALITY (purpose – value capture → durable revenue)
• Map revenue architecture by model (subscription, license, usage, transaction, hardware,
services, advertising, marketplace) and state the revenue *unit* for each line.
• Identify price meters and prove they correlate with delivered customer value.
• Show gross and contribution margin by line and sensitivity to mix shift.
• Describe revenue recognition policy, seasonality patterns, and the roles of bookings,
backlog, and Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO).
• Quantify visibility—contracted, recurring, re-occurring, non-recurring—and concentration
by customer, product, channel, geography.
• Explain external demand drivers (macro cycles, ad markets, commodity inputs, interest-rate
sensitivity, regulatory constraints) that can swing volumes.
• List 2–3 leading KPIs per model that predict revenue one to two quarters ahead and show
empirical lead-lag.
• If payments/credit apply, add activity levels, take rate, cost stack, loss rates, and who bears credit/fraud risk.
• Identify the price meter best aligned with value that can scale 10× without raising churn.
• Flag any revenue line that carries negative optionality or cannibalizes a higher-margin
line.

10) PRICING POWER AND ELASTICITY TESTING (purpose – value capture)
• Document pricing governance—list vs realized price history, discount band discipline,
approval thresholds, and price fences.
• Present elasticity evidence from controlled price tests, cohort outcomes, win/loss data,
and cross-price effects.
• Summarize willingness-to-pay research (conjoint or van Westendorp), key buyer value
drivers, and sensitivity by industry/size.
• Explain packaging strategy—good-better-best tiers, bundle attach, usage/overage meters—and
leakage guardrails.
• Provide a monetization-change log of pricing/packaging/metering moves and realized impact.
• State reference price and switching cost (dollars/hours) by segment to ground barriers.
• Estimate ARPU ceiling before churn inflects and cite supporting evidence.

11) UNIT ECONOMICS AND EFFICIENCY (purpose – profitable scalability)
• Report CAC, payback period, magic number, and LTV/CAC by segment—stated or transparently inferred.
• Show contribution margin by line (software, usage, services) to reveal variable profit.
• Track cohort profitability and cumulative cash contribution over time to evidence
unit-level returns.
• Quantify implementation, onboarding, and support cost over lifetime to fully load
economics.
• Identify structurally unprofitable cohorts and whether strategy is fix or exit.
• Name the main constraint blocking a 20–30 % payback improvement and the remedy.
12) FINANCIAL PROFILE (purpose – operations → financial outcomes)
• Break down revenue mix and growth by component and gross margin by line, then show the
operating-leverage path.
• Present Rule-of-40 score and a GAAP-to-cash-flow bridge to reconcile accounting with liquidity.
• Highlight leading indicators (billings, RPO, backlog) that foreshadow revenue.
• Detail stock-based-compensation, dilution, and share-count trajectory.
• Explain liquidity needs, working-capital profile, and path to FCF breakeven and target
margin.
• State operational milestones required to hit target FCF margin and timeline.
• Flag accounting judgments that could swing EBIT by > 200 bps and show sensitivity.
• Compute the FCF/share CAGR needed to reach mid fair value and assess feasibility.
13) CAPITAL STRUCTURE AND COST OF CAPITAL (purpose – funding flexibility and risk)
• Detail the debt stack—instrument types, fixed/floating mix, hedges, covenants, collateral, maturities, amortization, prepay terms—to surface refinancing risk.
• Quantify leverage and coverage (gross/net, interest-coverage, Debt/EBITDA vs covenant
headroom) and stress for higher rates and lower EBITDA.
• Estimate WACC—capital-structure weights, risk-free rate, beta, equity risk premium,
credit spread—and show sensitivities.
• Summarize rating-agency posture and triggers and compare to management targets.
• Map equity plumbing—authorized vs issued, converts, buybacks, dividend policy, ATM,
option/RSU overhang—to project dilution.
• Identify funding shock or rate level that forces a strategy shift or covenant breach and
outline the contingency plan.
• State headroom to fund growth at target leverage while preserving ratings.
• Define liquidity runway and covenant headroom thresholds that force Sell or Wait.

14) MOAT AND DATA ADVANTAGE (purpose – defensibility)
• Explain workflow depth and proprietary data that create lock-in.
• Analyze network or ecosystem effects, showing how value strengthens with scale.
• Demonstrate measurable analytics or AI advantages that translate to outcomes.
• Map integration footprint and practical switching costs across adjacent systems.
• Provide evidence the moat is deepening over time, not static or eroding.
• Identify the event most likely to collapse the moat within two years and estimate its
probability.

15) DATA AND ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE ECONOMICS (purpose – margin drivers)
• Describe data sources, ownership rights, exclusivity, consent provenance, refresh cadence,
and quality controls that underpin AI.
• Quantify labeling/curation costs, model-training compute, per-inference cost, and
unit-cost decline roadmap.
• Assess vendor and IP risk—model or infrastructure dependencies, portability, open-/closed-source posture, patent coverage, and freedom-to-operate.
• Outline evaluation framework—offline/online tests, attributable KPIs, guardrails,
drift-detection, rollback policies—to ensure model quality.
• Evaluate data-moat mechanics—uniqueness, scale, timeliness, feedback loops—separate from
general network effects.
• Describe the self-reinforcing data loop and contractual protection for
rights/consent/exclusivity.
• Estimate marginal ROI of each AI feature versus a non-AI baseline and how ROI scales.

16) EXECUTION QUALITY AND ORGANIZATION (purpose – operating cadence)
• Summarize leadership track record, stability, organizational design, and succession
readiness.
• Report engineering velocity—release cadence, defect and incident rates—where data exist.
• Triangulate customer sentiment using CSAT, NPS, peer reviews, and community signals.
• Flag a single leadership gap that is existential within 12–24 months and outline the
succession or hire plan.
• Name the operating-cadence metric that best predicts misses and describe how it triggers
action.

17) SUPPLY CHAIN AND OPERATIONS (purpose – fulfilment and cost risk; include if
hardware/services heavy)
• List critical suppliers, single-source exposures, top-5 concentration, capacity
commitments, lead times, yields, and quality escapes.
• Provide field performance—warranty accruals vs claims, RMA rates/roots, refurbishment recovery, inventory turns, aging, and obsolescence reserves.
• Describe logistics/continuity—key lanes, 3PL dependencies, regional diversification,
tariff/export-control exposure, dual-sourcing and disaster-recovery plans.
• Explain manufacturing economics—make-vs-buy logic, contract-manufacturer terms,
learning-curve slope, utilization breakevens.
• If services are material, show staffing levels, utilization, backlog, SLA attainment, and
margin by tier.
• Identify the single point of failure and quantify time/cost to dual-source it.
• Compare cost-curve and yield learning rate versus peers and note what would change the slope.

18) RISK INVENTORY AND MITIGANTS (purpose – make downside explicit)
• Prioritize macro, regulatory, competitive, operational, and concentration risks with plain
impact descriptions.
• Include payments, credit, or compliance risks if the model warrants.
• Highlight implementation complexity and time-to-value risk with realistic timelines.
• Lead with indicators and mitigations; cross-reference covenant/liquidity metrics (Section 13)
and supply-chain continuity (Section 17).
• Name the top 12-month risk, quantify P&L impact, and outline a recovery playbook.
• Define an objective stop-loss or escalation trigger that forces capital preservation.

19) MERGERS AND ACQUISITIONS STRATEGY AND OPTIONALITY (purpose – non-organic growth)
• Review past deals versus plan—revenue, margin, cash-flow, synergy capture, post-merger
churn, integration cost.
• Apply a build-buy-partner framework to close roadmap gaps with evidence.
• Assess integration muscle—playbooks, platform convergence, leadership retention, cultural integration, systems/process harmonization.
• Summarize financing mix, valuation discipline versus comps, earn-outs/contingent
consideration, and impairment history.
• Describe M&A pipeline, regulatory environment, and how acquisitions shift competitive
dynamics and thesis risk.
• Identify capability gaps that cannot be built organically in time and why acquisition is
needed.

20) VALUATION FRAMEWORK (purpose – value with cross-checks)
• Establish an outside-view baseline using peer medians/IQR for growth, margins, reinvestment, and valuation; justify deviations.
• Present a public-comps table—growth, gross margin, operating margin, Rule-of-40,
EV/Revenue, EV/Gross Profit—normalized for disclosure quirks.
• Build a discounted-cash-flow (DCF) with explicit drivers and sensitivity bands to show
value swing.
• Run a reverse-DCF to surface market-implied growth, margins, reinvestment and explain
where you disagree.
• Output a fair-value band (low/mid/high) and required {MOS_%} margin-of-safety to act.
• Benchmark current multiple versus 5-year peer percentile and only recommend Buy if a
credible re-rating path exists.
• Cross-check value with cohort NPV math, adoption S-curves, and unit-economics-to-EV sanity
checks.
• For private names, triangulate valuation using last-round terms, secondary indications,
and revenue multiples.
• State market-implied expectations from the reverse-DCF and the single variable explaining
most dispersion.

21) SCENARIOS, CATALYSTS, AND MONITORING PLAN (purpose – expectations and triggers)
• Build 12–24 month bear, base, and bull cases—NRR, new-logo adds, pricing/take rate,
margins, SBC, share count—with probabilities summing to 100 %.
• Compute probability-weighted E[TR] and block Buy if below {HURDLE_TR_%}.
• Lead with bear path: bear price/drawdown, recovery path, and time to recoup.
• Perform a reverse stress test with hard triggers, a stress price band, and
pre-committed downgrade/re-entry rules.
• List near-term catalysts with firm dates and quantified impact on key numbers or multiple.
• Provide an entry plan with buy/add/trim/exit bands tied to price and thesis-break metrics.
• Monitor early warnings—small-cohort churn spikes, backlog slippage, uptime incidents,
pricing pushback—with clear symptom → action mapping.
• Define stop/review levels when metrics breach or price hits bear band without catalyst
progress.
• Rank expected return per unit downside versus two realistic alternatives to surface opportunity cost.
• End with three positive and three negative “change-my-mind” triggers that would flip the
rating.

MODELING INSTRUCTIONS (simple but defensible)
• Build revenue by segment/product; if usage-based, include volume & take-rate drivers.
• Estimate gross margin by line; set operating-expense ratios and SBC; output free-cash-flow.
• Provide share-count & dilution schedule for the next eight quarters (public names).
• Include two-way sensitivity tables on the two most material drivers.
• Reconcile GAAP operating loss to FCF with a clear bridge.
RATING LOGIC — assign Buy / Hold / Wait-for-entry / Sell strictly per Decision rules.
QUALITY BAR — back key statements with numbers & citations; label speculation **Inference**;
prefer bullets & tables; keep prose tight.

The Supreme Court hears the Digital News Publishers Association's challenge to the DPDP Act tomorrow, 17 November 2026.

The petition challenges sections 7, 17(2), 18, 19, 27, 29, 36, 37 and 44(3) of the Act and Rules 16, 17 and 23 of the DPDP Rules. Senior Advocate Madhavi Divan argued for DNPA on 27 October that the consent requirements could disrupt the work of newsrooms.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana issued notice on the petition and the stay application on 27 October. The court did not stay any provision.

Since then, the News Broadcasters & Digital Association has written to the IT Minister for a journalism exemption, and unnamed government sources told PTI on 7 November that journalists are not Data Fiduciaries. By my reading, none of this has changed the text of the Act.

Of the challenged provisions, sections 18, 19 and 44(3) and Rule 17 are already in force. Most of the others start on 13 May 2027.

Bangladesh Islami Chhatrashibir has expressed deep concern over the removal of nearly 130 million names from India's nationwide electoral rolls through the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process, warning that the voting rights and citizenship security of a significant number of eligible Muslim voters could be jeopardised. Central President Nurul Islam and Secretary General Sibgatullah voiced this concern in a joint statement issued today, 16 November (Monday).

In the statement, the leaders noted: "According to reports published by various international and local media outlets, the proportion of Muslims among those excluded from India's nationwide electoral roll revision process is disproportionately high. In West Bengal alone, approximately 2.7 million voters have been excluded following the adjudication process under the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), nearly 70 per cent of whom are Muslims. Despite possessing valid identity documents and family records, many Bengali-speaking Muslims have had their names removed from the electoral rolls. There have also been allegations that, in the course of this process, many of them are being detained on accusations of being 'illegal infiltrators' and forcibly expelled into Bangladesh. Such actions constitute clear violations of international human rights conventions."

Referring to India's existing electoral and constitutional framework, the leaders emphasised: "Under Section 21(3) of India's Representation of the People Act, 1950, the Election Commission of India (ECI) is empowered to direct a special revision of electoral rolls. However, Section 22 of the same Act and Rule 21A of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, require proper verification of information, a reasonable opportunity for the individuals concerned to present their cases, and decisions in accordance with established legal procedures before any name is removed from the electoral rolls. Furthermore, Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution of India guarantee equality before the law and prohibit discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth, respectively. Therefore, curtailing any citizen's voting rights or subjecting them to discriminatory treatment on the basis of religious identity runs contrary to the constitutional principles of the country."

The statement also highlighted the broader pattern of discrimination against Muslims in India, with the leaders observing: "The process of restricting the civil and fundamental rights of Muslims in India is not an isolated incident; rather, it is part of a long-term state and legal agenda. The controversial Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) and the National Register of Citizens (NRC) have facilitated the development of a discriminatory framework for determining citizenship on the basis of religious identity. In addition, measures and actions such as the abrogation of Article 370, the law on triple talaq, attempts to impose a Uniform Civil Code (UCC), the Waqf property amendment law, restrictions imposed by various states on cow slaughter and beef consumption, the demolition of mosques, and the demolition of Muslim homes and other structures using bulldozers have undermined the religious, social, and economic rights of Muslims. The current electoral roll revision process is a clear manifestation of this continuing pattern of discriminatory measures, reflecting a policy of 'identify, exclude and expel.'"

Emphasising the fundamental responsibility of the state to protect the rights of its citizens, the leaders declared: "Ensuring citizens' voting rights and security is one of the primary responsibilities of any state. Depriving any community of its voting rights or subjecting its members to harassment over questions of citizenship on the basis of their religious identity is wholly unacceptable.

We strongly urge the Government of the Republic of India to immediately halt the discriminatory removal of names from the electoral rolls, reinstate the names of genuine and eligible voters, and cease unlawful detentions and the forcible expulsion of individuals into Bangladesh."

The leaders also called upon the international community to abandon double standards in the application of human rights principles. They urged the United Nations, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), and international human rights organisations to take effective measures to safeguard the fundamental human rights and civil rights of Muslims belonging to India's minority community.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.
